title: The Desert Messenger
summary: A young messenger named Salim must cross the desert by camel to bring a healer to his sick town leader, managing his water and pace wisely and sheltering from a sandstorm along the way.
poll: A traveler should always push forward instead of stopping to wait out danger.

versions.title: The Desert Messenger
versions.text:
Salim is a messenger. He lives in Najim. It is a desert town.

The leader of Najim is sick. A healer can help him. The healer lives in Dirah.

Salim must take a letter there. He rides his camel, Badr. He packs food and water. Then he starts his journey.

It is hot and dry. Salim rides when it is cool. He rests at noon. The sun is too hot then.

One day, the sky turns dark. The wind blows hard. A storm is near! Salim finds shelter. He hides by a big rock.

The storm ends. Salim rides on. At night, he looks up. He sees the stars. They show him the way.

Salim gets to Dirah. He is just in time. He gives the letter to the healer. The healer gets on his camel. They ride back to help the sick leader.

versions.title: The Desert Messenger

Salim is a messenger. He lives in Najim, a desert town. The leader there is sick. A healer in Dirah can help him.

Salim must take a letter to Dirah. He saddles his camel, Badr. He packs food and water. Then he begins his journey.

The desert is hot and dry. Salim rides when the air is cool. He rests when the sun gets too hot. He waits until it cools again.

One day, the sky turns dark. The wind starts to blow hard. A sandstorm is coming fast! Salim quickly finds shelter. He hides behind a big rock.

At last, the storm ends. Salim climbs back onto Badr. At night, he looks up at the stars. They show him which way to go.

Salim reaches Dirah just in time. He hands the letter to the healer. The healer jumps onto his camel. Together, they ride back to help the sick leader.

versions.title: The Desert Messenger
versions.text:
Salim is a young messenger. He lives in Najim, a small desert town. The leader there has fallen sick. Only a healer in Dirah can help him.

Salim must carry an important letter to Dirah. He saddles his fast camel, Badr. He packs enough food and water for the journey. Then he sets off into the desert.

The desert is hot and very dry. Salim rides quickly when the air is cool. He rests once the sun grows too hot at noon. He waits in whatever shade he can find.

One afternoon, the sky begins to turn dark. The wind starts to blow hard. A sandstorm is coming fast! Salim quickly guides Badr behind a large rock. They wait there for shelter.

At last, the storm passes. Salim climbs back onto Badr. At night, he looks up at the bright stars. They show him which way to go.

Salim reaches Dirah just as the sun sets. He arrives just in time. He hands the letter to the healer. The healer quickly jumps onto his own camel. Together, they ride back to help the sick leader.

versions.title: The Desert Messenger
versions.text:
Salim is a young messenger who lives in the small desert town of Najim. The town's leader has suddenly fallen very sick. Only a skilled healer who lives in the distant town of Dirah can help him.

Salim is given the task of carrying an important letter to Dirah. He saddles his fastest camel, Badr. He packs enough food and water for the journey. Carefully, he tucks the letter inside his robe.

The desert sun is merciless. The sand offers little shade. Salim rides quickly while the air is cool in the morning and evening. He rests once the midday sun grows too hot to bear.

One afternoon, the sky begins to turn a dusty, dark shade. A hot wind suddenly starts to blow hard. Salim recognizes the warning signs of a sandstorm. He quickly guides Badr behind a large rock to find shelter from the storm.

When the wind finally dies down, Salim climbs back onto Badr. He rides on. At night, he finds his way by the bright stars overhead. They guide him safely across the dark desert.

Salim finally reaches Dirah just as the sun is setting. He arrives just in time. He hands the letter to the healer. The healer quickly saddles his own camel. Together, they ride back to help the sick leader.

versions.title: The Desert Messenger
versions.text:
Salim is a young messenger who lives in the small desert town of Najim. The town's leader has suddenly fallen gravely ill. Only a skilled healer who lives in the distant town of Dirah, three days away by camel, can cure him.

The town elders choose Salim for this urgent task. He knows the desert routes well and rides with a steady pace. He saddles his swiftest camel, Badr, and packs enough water and food to endure the journey. He tucks the letter carefully inside his robe.

The desert sun is merciless, and the sand offers almost no shade. Salim keeps a brisk pace during the cool hours of morning and evening. He slows to rest once the midday sun becomes unbearable. Twice along the way, he stops at a small oasis to refill his water and let Badr drink.

One afternoon, the sky turns a dusty, dark shade. A hot wind suddenly rises. Salim recognizes these as warning signs of a sandstorm. Rather than racing ahead, he guides Badr behind a rocky outcrop and waits for the fierce wind to die down.

When the storm passes, Salim climbs back onto Badr and rides on. That night, he finds his way by the bright stars, trusting them to guide him across the dark desert.

Salim reaches Dirah just as the sun sets on the third day, arriving just in time. He learns the healer was about to leave on another journey. If Salim had come a day later, no one would have been there to help. He hands over the letter, and the healer saddles his camel so they can ride back together to save the sick leader.

versions.title: The Desert Messenger
versions.text:
Salim, a young messenger from the small desert town of Najim, is entrusted with an extraordinarily vital task when the town's leader suddenly falls gravely ill: only a skilled healer residing in the distant town of Dirah, a formidable three days away by camel across an unforgiving expanse of open desert, possesses the specialized knowledge required to cure him.

The town elders select Salim for this mission because he comprehends the desert routes better than almost anyone his age and is capable of maintaining a steady, disciplined pace for hours without succumbing to fatigue. He meticulously saddles his swiftest camel, Badr, loading sufficient water and provisions to sustain the entirety of the journey, and tucks the folded letter carefully inside his robe so that it cannot be lost or irreparably damaged along the arduous way.

The merciless desert sun offers scarcely any shade whatsoever, so Salim maintains a brisk pace during the comparatively cool hours of morning and evening while slowing to rest once the midday heat becomes altogether unbearable, since riding too vigorously in such punishing conditions could exhaust both rider and camel alike. He carefully rations his water, taking small, deliberate sips rather than large, wasteful gulps, and twice along the route he pauses at a small oasis, where date palms grow beside a hidden spring, to replenish his water skins before pressing onward into the merciless sand.

One afternoon, a hot wind suddenly rises across the dunes, violently stirring loose sand into the choking air, and Salim immediately recognizes these as the unmistakable warning signs of an approaching sandstorm. Rather than racing ahead and risking becoming hopelessly and perhaps fatally lost among the blinding, swirling sand, he guides Badr behind a rocky outcrop and waits with remarkable patience until the fierce wind eventually subsides, covering both his own and Badr's faces to keep out the stinging, abrasive grit.

When the storm finally passes, Salim presses onward through the cooling night air, navigating by the bright stars overhead and trusting the ancient patterns he learned as a boy to guide him safely and unerringly across the darkened, silent desert.

Salim reaches Dirah precisely as the sun sets on the third day, arriving exactly in time: the healer had already packed his belongings, preparing to depart for another town at dawn, and had Salim arrived even a single day later, no one whatsoever would have remained to help the sick leader. He hands over the letter without delay, and the healer, perusing it swiftly, immediately saddles his own camel so the two of them can race back together to save him.

Salim's meticulous planning, measured pace, and patient judgment during the sandstorm ultimately proved every bit as crucial as his raw speed, illustrating convincingly that a prudent traveler who recognizes precisely when to wait often arrives sooner, in the final analysis, than one who recklessly presses onward through genuine danger.

keyWords.definition: a person who carries a message from one place to another
keyWords.example: The king sent a messenger to tell the village the news.

keyWords.definition: a large desert animal that can travel long distances without water
keyWords.example: Our family rode a camel across the sandy hills.

keyWords.definition: a very dry, sandy place that gets almost no rain
keyWords.example: We packed extra water before driving through the desert.

keyWords.definition: a long trip from one place to another
keyWords.example: Our journey to the coast took all day.

keyWords.definition: a safe place that protects you from danger or bad weather
keyWords.example: We found shelter under a tree when it began to rain.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: A young boy who learns to build small wooden fishing boats
A messenger who crosses the desert to bring help for a sick leader
A girl who takes care of camels in a small village market
A traveling merchant who sells water and cloth in town
questions.why: The story follows Salim as he rides across the desert to bring a healer to help the sick leader of Najim.

wrong.A: No one builds a boat in this story.
wrong.C: The story is about a messenger, not a girl tending camels.
wrong.D: Salim does not sell water; he carries a letter.

questions.stem: Why does Salim travel to Dirah?
options: To buy himself a brand-new, faster camel from the market
To visit his family during a holiday in the town
To trade some food for extra water at the well
To bring a letter asking for help from a healer
questions.why: The story says Salim must take a letter to Dirah to ask the healer to help the sick leader.

wrong.A: Salim already has a camel, Badr.
wrong.B: The story does not say Salim has family in Dirah.
wrong.C: Salim does not trade food for water.

questions.stem: What does Salim do at midday?
options: He rests because the sun is too hot
He rides even faster than before
He swims and plays in an oasis
He sleeps the whole day away
questions.why: The story says the sun at noon is too hot, so Salim rests then and rides again when it is cool.

wrong.B: Salim slows down, not speeds up, at midday.
wrong.C: The story does not mention swimming.
wrong.D: Salim only rests, not sleeps all day.

questions.stem: In the story, what does shelter mean?
options: a kind of fast desert camel
an old letter from the leader
a safe place to wait out danger
a strong and dusty sandstorm
questions.why: Salim finds shelter behind a rock, meaning a safe place where he waits out the sandstorm.

wrong.D: Shelter is a safe place, not the storm itself.

questions.stem: Why does Salim stop behind the rock when the sandstorm comes?
options: He is tired and wants to sleep for a while in the shade
He wants to protect himself and Badr from the storm
He forgot the way to the town of Dirah in the storm
The rock is cooler than the sand around it in the desert
questions.why: A sandstorm is dangerous, so stopping behind the rock keeps Salim and Badr safe until it passes.

wrong.A: The story does not say Salim is tired.
wrong.C: Salim still knows the way after the storm.
wrong.D: The story does not compare the temperature of the rock and sand.

questions.stem: What can you tell about Salim from the story?
options: He is careless and reckless
He does not like camels
He is afraid of the desert and refuses to go
He is calm and makes wise choices
questions.why: Salim rests when it is too hot, shelters wisely from the storm, and still reaches Dirah in time, showing good judgment.

wrong.A: A careless rider would not plan his rest and shelter so carefully.
wrong.B: Salim relies on and cares for his camel, Badr.
wrong.C: Salim bravely makes the journey across the desert.

questions.stem: What happens because the sky turns dark and the wind blows hard?
options: Salim decides to shelter from a sandstorm
Salim rides faster to escape the storm
Badr runs away from the dark sky
The healer leaves the town of Dirah
questions.why: The dark sky and strong wind are warning signs of a sandstorm, so Salim finds shelter behind a rock.

wrong.B: Salim shelters instead of racing ahead.
wrong.C: Badr stays with Salim the whole time.
wrong.D: The healer is still in Dirah when Salim arrives.

questions.stem: Why does the author tell us Salim rests at noon and rides when it is cool?
options: To show that Salim does not like camels very much
To describe Dirah's buildings and its busy streets
To show how he wisely manages the desert heat
To explain why camels need water on long trips
questions.why: Describing Salim's pattern of riding and resting shows that he carefully manages the heat to finish his journey safely.

wrong.A: This detail is about heat, not camels.
wrong.B: The story does not describe buildings in Dirah.
wrong.D: This detail is about Salim's pace, not Badr's water needs.

LOW.prompt: Would you want to be a desert messenger like Salim? Explain why or why not, using at least two facts from the story.
checklist: I clearly said what I think.
I used at least two facts from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: I would want to be a desert messenger like Salim. I would like riding a camel named Badr across the desert. I would also feel proud to deliver an important letter that helps a sick leader. I know a sandstorm could be scary, but Salim found shelter behind a rock and stayed safe.

keyWords.definition: a place in the desert with water and plants, often with a spring
keyWords.example: The tired travelers rested at an oasis surrounded by palm trees.

keyWords.definition: the speed at which someone moves or does something
keyWords.example: The runner kept a steady pace for the whole race.

keyWords.definition: needing quick action because it is very important
keyWords.example: The nurse rushed to answer the urgent call for help.

keyWords.definition: to keep going through something difficult
keyWords.example: The hikers had to endure a long climb up the mountain.

keyWords.definition: a part of rock that sticks out from the ground or a hillside
keyWords.example: The climbers rested on a flat outcrop of stone.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the story?
options: Salim races across the desert on a swift camel, using careful planning and good judgment to deliver a life-saving letter just in time.
Salim gets lost in a terrible sandstorm and never manages to reach the town of Dirah at all, and the letter is lost.
Salim is simply a desert merchant who travels around selling water to thirsty travelers, and he has no letter to bring.
Camels are described as being the fastest and strongest animals living anywhere in the desert, and the story is about their speed.
questions.why: The story focuses on Salim's careful planning, pace, and patience as he crosses the desert to deliver an urgent letter in time to save the sick leader.

wrong.B: Salim shelters from the storm and continues his journey safely.
wrong.C: Salim is a messenger, not a merchant.
wrong.D: The story is not about comparing animal speeds.

questions.stem: Why do the town elders choose Salim for this task?
options: He is simply the only person in Najim who happens to own a camel
He knows the desert routes well and can keep a steady pace
He is the son of the town's sick leader, so he feels he must go
He has visited the town of Dirah many, many times before this trip
questions.why: The story says the elders choose Salim because he knows the desert routes and rides with a steady pace.

wrong.A: The story does not say Salim is the only camel owner.
wrong.C: The story does not say Salim is related to the leader.
wrong.D: The story does not mention earlier visits to Dirah.

questions.stem: About how long does the journey to Dirah take?
options: One day
A week
A single night
Three days
questions.why: The story says Dirah is three long days away by camel, and Salim arrives on the third day.

wrong.A: The journey takes much longer than one day.
wrong.B: The story says three days, not a week.
wrong.C: The journey includes rest stops across several days, not just one night.

questions.stem: In the passage, what does endure mean?
options: to enjoy something briefly, then stop
to give something away to a friend
to keep going despite difficulty
to measure distance with a long ruler
questions.why: Salim packs enough water and food to endure the entire journey, meaning to keep going through its difficulty.

wrong.A: Endure means to keep going, not to enjoy briefly.
wrong.B: Endure is not about giving something away.
wrong.D: Endure does not mean measuring distance.

questions.stem: Why does Salim stop at an oasis along the way?
options: To rest for a while simply because he feels bored
To refill his water and let Badr drink before continuing
To meet and talk with other desert travelers passing by
To wait out the worst heat of the midday sun there
questions.why: An oasis has water, so Salim stops there to refill his water skins and let Badr drink before pressing on.

wrong.A: The story does not say Salim is bored.
wrong.C: The story does not mention meeting other travelers.
wrong.D: Salim rests from noon heat separately, in whatever shade he finds, not specifically at the oasis.

questions.stem: Why is arriving exactly on the third day so important?
options: The healer was about to leave Dirah for another journey
The important letter would lose all of its meaning after three full days
Badr the camel could not possibly travel for longer than three days
The town elders simply set a three-day limit just for fun
questions.why: The story explains that if Salim had arrived even a day later, the healer would have already left on another journey.

wrong.B: The story does not say the letter expires.
wrong.C: The story does not set a travel limit for Badr.
wrong.D: The three-day timing is tied to the healer's departure, not a rule made for fun.

questions.stem: What does Salim do when he notices the dusty sky and rising wind?
options: He rides faster to outrun the storm and reach town
He turns back toward Najim at once, to find his family
He ignores the signs and keeps going on his way
He shelters behind a rocky outcrop and waits
questions.why: Recognizing the warning signs of a sandstorm, Salim guides Badr behind a rocky outcrop and waits for the storm to pass.

wrong.A: Salim does not try to outrun the storm.
wrong.B: Salim continues toward Dirah, not back toward Najim.
wrong.C: Salim pays close attention to the warning signs instead of ignoring them.

questions.stem: How is Salim's choice to shelter different from simply racing ahead through the storm?
options: Both of these two choices are equally risky for Salim in the middle of a storm
Sheltering protects him from getting lost or hurt, while racing ahead risks disaster
Racing ahead through a sandstorm is faster and also much safer than waiting
There is no real difference at all between these two choices for Salim
questions.why: The story explains that racing ahead risks getting lost, while sheltering behind the outcrop keeps Salim and Badr safe until the storm passes.

wrong.A: The story presents sheltering as the much safer choice.
wrong.C: Racing ahead is riskier, not safer.
wrong.D: The two choices lead to very different outcomes.

MID.prompt: Explain how Salim manages his water, his pace, and the danger of the sandstorm during his journey. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained how Salim manages at least two of these: water, pace, or the storm.
I used at least two details from the story.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: Salim manages his journey very carefully. He keeps a brisk pace in the cool morning and evening but rests when the midday sun becomes unbearable. He also stops at an oasis twice to refill his water and let Badr drink. When he notices the warning signs of a sandstorm, he does not race ahead; instead, he shelters behind a rocky outcrop until the wind dies down, which keeps him safe and lets him reach Dirah just in time.

keyWords.definition: to find your way from one place to another
keyWords.example: Sailors used to navigate by watching the position of the stars.

keyWords.definition: to use something carefully in small amounts so it lasts longer
keyWords.example: The hikers had to ration their food during the long trail.

keyWords.definition: extremely important, often necessary for survival or success
keyWords.example: Clean water is vital for staying healthy.

keyWords.definition: very careful and paying close attention to every detail
keyWords.example: The mechanic was meticulous when checking every part of the engine.

keyWords.definition: to fill something back up after it has been used
keyWords.example: We stopped at the store to replenish our supply of water bottles.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the passage?
options: Salim's careful judgment, pacing, and endurance allow him to deliver a vital message across the desert just in time to save a life.
The desert is presented in the passage as being impossible for anyone to cross safely under any circumstances whatsoever.
Camels are described throughout the passage as requiring very little water to survive even the longest journeys.
Sandstorms are described in the passage as posing no real danger at all to experienced desert travelers.
questions.why: The passage centers on Salim's disciplined pace, careful rationing, and wise decision to shelter, all of which allow him to arrive in time to save the sick leader.

wrong.B: Salim successfully crosses the desert, showing it can be done with care.
wrong.C: The passage does not focus on the camel's water needs.
wrong.D: The passage treats the sandstorm as genuinely dangerous.

questions.stem: According to the passage, how does Salim manage his water supply?
options: He drinks freely and without any real restraint whenever he happens to feel thirsty
He carries no water at all with him and relies entirely on desert plants instead
He trades some of his water with other desert travelers along the way
He rations his water, taking small sips, and replenishes it at oases
questions.why: The passage states that Salim carefully rations his water and replenishes his water skins at oases along the route.

wrong.A: Salim is deliberate about his water use, not careless.
wrong.B: Salim carries water skins with him.
wrong.C: The passage does not mention trading water with others.

questions.stem: What does Salim discover upon arriving in Dirah?
options: The healer had already left the town of Dirah for good, long ago
The healer was about to depart for another town at dawn
The leader of Najim had, in fact, already fully recovered on his own
Dirah had also been struck hard by that very same fierce sandstorm
questions.why: The passage explains that the healer had already packed his bags, preparing to leave for another town at dawn.

wrong.A: The healer is still in Dirah when Salim arrives.
wrong.C: The leader is still sick, which is why the letter is urgent.
wrong.D: The passage does not say the storm reached Dirah.

questions.stem: In the passage, the word meticulously most nearly means —
options: in a careless, hurried, and rather sloppy manner
without stopping to do any planning at all beforehand
with great care and attention to detail
in a reluctant, slow, and rather unwilling manner
questions.why: Salim meticulously saddles his camel and packs his supplies, meaning he does it with great care and attention to detail.

wrong.A: Meticulously means the opposite of careless.
wrong.B: Meticulously implies careful planning, not its absence.
wrong.D: The passage does not suggest Salim is reluctant or slow.

questions.stem: Why does Salim choose to shelter behind the outcrop rather than race ahead of the sandstorm?
options: He underestimates how dangerous the storm could be to him and Badr
He recognizes that pressing on risks becoming lost or losing vital supplies
He is simply too exhausted to continue at all after walking the whole day
Badr refuses to move any farther along the dry trail, so they stop
questions.why: The passage shows Salim weighing the danger of the storm and choosing the safer option of shelter over the risk of pressing on blindly.

wrong.A: Salim takes the storm's danger seriously, which is why he shelters.
wrong.C: The passage does not say Salim is too exhausted to continue.
wrong.D: The passage does not say Badr refuses to move.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about why the town elders selected Salim rather than another rider?
options: He simply happened to be the only available rider in town that particular day, so the elders chose him
He was known throughout Najim as being, by far, the single wealthiest person, so the elders trusted his money
His familiarity with the desert routes and his disciplined pace make him uniquely suited to the task
He had never once ridden a camel before, so he badly needed the practice that this long ride would give
questions.why: The passage emphasizes Salim's knowledge of the desert routes and his steady, disciplined pace as the reasons he is chosen for this vital task.

wrong.A: The passage gives specific reasons beyond mere availability.
wrong.B: Wealth is never mentioned as a factor.
wrong.D: Salim is clearly an experienced rider, not a beginner.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly orders the events in the passage?
options: The storm passes, then the storm begins, then Salim reaches Dirah, and the healer waits for him in town
Salim reaches Dirah, then the storm begins, then he shelters behind the outcrop, and then he leaves Najim
The healer departs for another town, then Salim arrives in Dirah, then he shelters from the sandstorm at last
Salim departs from Najim, then shelters from the sandstorm, then reaches Dirah just as the healer prepares to leave
questions.why: Salim first leaves Najim, then encounters and shelters from the sandstorm along the way, and finally arrives in Dirah just as the healer is preparing to depart.

wrong.A: The storm begins before it passes, not the reverse.
wrong.B: Salim encounters the storm before reaching Dirah, not after.
wrong.C: The healer has not yet departed when Salim arrives.

questions.stem: Why does the passage emphasize that a 'wise traveler who knows when to wait' often arrives sooner than one who presses on recklessly?
options: To suggest that patience and good judgment can be more valuable than raw speed
To argue that waiting is always better than moving, even when a storm is far away
To criticize Salim for being too slow and for stopping at noon each day
To explain why camels need rest and water after long days in the heat
questions.why: This closing idea highlights that Salim's patient, careful decisions, not just his speed, are what allow him to succeed.

wrong.B: The passage does not claim waiting is always better, only that it was wise in this situation.
wrong.C: The passage praises, rather than criticizes, Salim's judgment.
wrong.D: This line is about human judgment, not a camel's need for rest.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says a traveler should always push forward instead of stopping to wait out danger. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from Salim's journey.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the passage.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I disagree that a traveler should always push forward instead of waiting out danger. Salim's journey shows why: when he notices the warning signs of a sandstorm, he chooses to shelter behind a rocky outcrop rather than race ahead, which protects him and Badr from becoming lost in the blinding sand. His careful rationing of water and disciplined pace also show that patience, not just speed, helped him arrive in time to save the sick leader. Someone might argue that stopping could have cost him precious time, but the passage makes clear that pressing on recklessly could have ended in disaster, so his patient judgment was truly the wiser choice.
